title: Gain-Bandwidth Trade-Offs
intro: For a one-pole amplifier, raising gain lowers bandwidth by the same factor. The product stays constant and is a better figure of merit than either alone. Cascading stages raises the product but shrinks the bandwidth.

blocks.text: A CS stage with a current-source load and load capacitance $C_L$ has DC gain $A_0 = g_{m1}(r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2})$ and output pole $\omega_p = 1/[(r_{o1} \parallel r_{o2})C_L]$. The output resistance cancels in their product:
For example $g_m = 1/(100\ \Omega)$ and $C_L = 50\text{ fF}$ give 31.8 GHz. The unity-gain frequency follows from $A_0/\sqrt{1 + (\omega_u/\omega_p)^2} = 1$:

so for one pole the unity-gain bandwidth equals the GBW. Cascoding does not help: it multiplies $R_{out}$, and so $A_0$, by some factor $K$ and divides the pole by the same $K$. The only levers are more $g_m$ (current or width) or less $C_L$, the heart of the speed-power trade-off. In nanometer devices a CS stage loaded by an identical stage reaches a GBW of a few tens of GHz, well below $f_T$.
Two identical stages in cascade (each $A_0$, pole $\omega_p$) give $A_0^2/(1 + s/\omega_p)^2$. Setting the magnitude to $A_0^2/\sqrt{2}$:
The product rises by $0.64A_0$ over a single stage (for twice the power), but the bandwidth itself falls. For $N$ identical stages

blocks.alt: Normalised gain in dB against frequency over pole frequency for one, two, three and four identical cascaded poles. The minus 3 dB points move from 1 to 0.64, 0.51 and 0.43, and the roll-off steepens with N.
blocks.caption: The bandwidth shrinks steadily as identical stages are cascaded.

blocks.text: Multiple poles also cost phase, which makes a cascade hard to stabilise inside a feedback loop.

blocks.title: GBW
blocks.text: $g_m = 2\text{ mS}$ and $C_L = 200\text{ fF}$. Find GBW and the $-3$ dB bandwidth when the gain is 20.
solution: At a gain of 20 the bandwidth is $1.59\text{ GHz}/20 = 80\text{ MHz}$.
blocks.answer: GBW = 1.6 GHz; bandwidth 80 MHz at gain 20.

blocks.title: Two identical poles
blocks.text: What is the $-3$ dB bandwidth of two identical cascaded one-pole stages, each with pole $f_p$?
solution: Total $|H| = \frac{1}{1 + (f/f_p)^2}$. The $-3$ dB point satisfies $1 + (f/f_p)^2 = \sqrt{2}$, so $f = f_p\sqrt{\sqrt{2} - 1} = 0.644 f_p$.

blocks.title: One stage or two?
blocks.text: You need a gain of 100. Option A: one stage with GBW = 2 GHz. Option B: two stages, each with gain 10 and pole 200 MHz (each also has GBW = 2 GHz). Compare the bandwidths.
solution: B: $0.644 \times 200\text{ MHz} = 129\text{ MHz}$, at twice the power.
blocks.answer: 20 MHz for one stage, 129 MHz for two.
